content: A printed circuit board (PCB) is a platform used to mechanically support and electrically connect electronic components. This is achieved through conductive pathways, or traces, which are etched from copper sheets laminated onto a non-conductive substrate. PCBs are also referred to as printed wiring boards (PWBs) or etched wiring boards. When electronic components are mounted onto a PCB, it becomes a printed circuit assembly (PCA) or a printed circuit board assembly (PCBA). PCBs are known for their durability, cost-effectiveness, and reliability, especially in high-volume production, although their initial design and layout require significant effort and expense compared to wire-wrapped or point-to-point constructed circuits. The electronics industry adheres to standards for PCB design, assembly, and quality control, which are published by the IPC organization. Manufacturing Materials The conductive layers in PCBs are typically made of thin copper foil. The insulating materials vary widely and include phenolic paper, glass fiber, and various plastics. PCB manufacturers often use prepregs, which are combinations of glass fiber mat, nonwoven material, and resin. These prepregs, along with copper foil, are laminated together using epoxy resin. Common prepreg materials in the PCB industry include FR-2 (phenolic cotton paper), FR-3 (cotton paper and epoxy), FR-4 (woven glass and epoxy), FR-5 (woven glass and epoxy), FR-6 (matte glass and polyester), G-10 (woven glass and epoxy), and CEM series materials (e.g., CEM-1, CEM-2, CEM-3, etc.). Patterning (Etching) Most PCBs are manufactured by bonding a layer of copper over the entire substrate, sometimes on both sides, to create a blank PCB. Unwanted copper is then removed using a temporary mask and etching techniques, leaving only the desired copper traces. Alternatively, some PCBs are made by adding traces to a bare substrate through complex electroplating processes. Subtractive methods, which remove copper, are the most common and include: Silk Screen Printing: Etch-resistant inks protect the copper foil, and subsequent etching removes unwanted copper. Conductive inks may also be printed on non-conductive boards. Photoengraving: A photomask and chemical etching are used to remove copper. Photomasks are prepared using photoplotters and CAM software, with laser-printed transparencies or direct laser imaging for high-resolution requirements. PCB Milling: A mechanical milling system removes copper foil from the substrate. This process uses a PCB prototyper, which operates like a plotter, controlled by software that positions the milling head. Additive processes, such as the semi-additive process, are also used. In this method, a thin copper layer is already present on the board, and a reverse mask is applied. Additional copper is plated onto the unmasked areas, followed by surface plating (e.g., tin-lead). The mask is then stripped, and a brief etching step removes the original copper laminate, isolating the traces. This process is common for multilayer boards as it facilitates plating-through of holes to create conductive vias. Lamination Multilayer PCBs, which have trace layers inside the board, are created by bonding together separately etched thin boards. Drilling Holes, or vias, are drilled into PCBs using tungsten carbide drill bits. Automated drilling machines, guided by computer-generated drill files (e.g., NCD or Excellon files), control the placement and size of each hole. For very small vias, laser drilling may be used, though it often results in inferior surface finishes. These small holes are called microvias. Controlled-depth drilling or pre-drilling individual PCB sheets before lamination can create blind vias (connecting an internal layer to an outer layer) or buried vias (connecting internal layers only). For boards with two or more layers, the walls of the holes are plated with copper to form plated-through holes, which electrically connect the conducting layers. Multilayer boards often require a chemical de-smear or plasma-etch process to remove bonding agent residue before plating. Exposed Conductor Plating and Coating Exposed copper areas, where components will be mounted, are typically plated to prevent oxidation and ensure solderability. Traditional plating involved tin-lead solder using hot air solder leveling (HASL). However, lead-free solder compounds are now used to comply with the EU's RoHS directive. Other plating options include organic surface protectants (OSP), immersion silver (IAg), immersion tin, electroless nickel with immersion gold (ENIG), and direct gold plating. Edge connectors on some boards are often gold-plated. Electrochemical migration (ECM) can occur under DC voltage bias, leading to the growth of conductive metal filaments on the PCB. Solder Resist Areas that should not be soldered are coated with a polymer solder resist (solder mask). This prevents solder bridging between conductors, which could cause short circuits, and provides environmental protection. Screen Printing Line art and text can be printed onto the outer surfaces of a PCB using screen printing. This text may indicate component designators, switch settings, test points, and other assembly or servicing information. Digital printing solutions are increasingly replacing traditional screen printing, allowing for variable data printing, such as serialization and barcodes for traceability. Testing Unpopulated boards undergo bare-board testing to verify circuit connections as defined in a netlist. High-volume production uses bed-of-nails testers or rigid needle adapters to make contact with copper lands or holes for testing. Computers direct electrical test units to send current through contact points and verify connectivity. Flying-probe testers are used for smallor medium-volume boards. Testing identifies shorts (unwanted connections) and opens (missing connections). In-circuit testing may also program nonvolatile memory components and exercise boundary scan test features of integrated circuits (ICs). Printed Circuit Assembly After PCB fabrication, electronic components are attached to create a functional printed circuit assembly (PCA). Through-hole construction involves inserting component leads into holes, while surface-mount construction places components on pads or lands on the PCB's surface. Components are fixed to the board using molten solder. Soldering techniques vary, and some components, like Ball Grid Array (BGA) packages, cannot be soldered by hand. Often, through-hole and surface-mount methods are combined in a single PCA for strength and space efficiency. Populated boards are tested using visual inspection, automated optical inspection, analog signature analysis, and functional tests to ensure proper operation. Protection and Packaging PCBs for extreme environments are coated with conformal coatings, such as silicone rubber, polyurethane, acrylic, or epoxy, to prevent corrosion and shorting due to condensation. Assembled PCBs are often static-sensitive and must be transported in antistatic bags. Proper grounding is essential when handling these boards to prevent damage from static discharge. Safety Certification (US) UL 796 safety standards cover requirements for PCBs used as components in devices or appliances. Testing evaluates characteristics like flammability, maximum operating temperature, electrical tracking, and heat deflection. Boards may use organic or inorganic base materials in rigid or flexible forms. Cordwood Construction Cordwood construction, used in space-constrained applications like missile guidance systems, involved mounting components axially between parallel planes and connecting them with nickel tapes welded to component leads. This method allowed high component density but required special nickel-leaded components. It has largely fallen out of use due to advancements in surface-mount technology and integrated circuits. Multiwire Boards Multiwire technology, used in the 1980s and 1990s, involved machine-routed insulated wires embedded in a non-conducting matrix. This approach simplified design by allowing direct wire connections but was cost-prohibitive for large-scale production. Surface-Mount Technology Surface-mount technology (SMT), developed in the 1960s and widely adopted by the 1990s, involves components with small metal tabs or end caps soldered directly to the PCB surface. SMT allows for smaller components, higher circuit densities, and automation, reducing labor costs and increasing production rates. Surface-mount devices (SMDs) are smaller, lighter, and often cheaper than through-hole components, though some exceptions exist. SMT has largely replaced through-hole technology for most applications.
